pair_convention.spot_explanation: CAD/JPY at 111.99 means 1 Canadian dollar buys 111.99 Japanese yen. A rising pair means CAD is strengthening versus JPY; a falling pair means CAD is weakening versus JPY. All pip references in this report are yen pips, where 0.01 equals 1 pip.

executive_summary: CAD/JPY trades at 111.99, having collapsed 3.74% in five sessions from the 116.47 high of 23 July as Japan's Ministry of Finance — for the first time since 2011 in coordination with the US Treasury — bought yen in size, with Japan's MoF spending an estimated $53 billion buying yen while the US Treasury sold euros and urged banks to act. The pair is down 2.96% over one month, 3.01% over three, 2.91% over six, and remains up just 1.91% over twelve — and it now sits 2.45% below its 200-day moving average at 114.81, having broken every major average in a single week. The dominant bilateral narrative is a collision the standalone dossiers cannot express: Canada is the G10's clearest terms-of-trade winner from a 31% Brent rally while Japan is its clearest loser, yet the pair has fallen anyway because the yen leg is now being driven by official intervention, a Bank of Japan 100bp below its own neutral estimate, and a positioning squeeze that has already fired. Three bilateral differentials diverge sharply from the standalone views: the BoC–BoJ policy gap of +125bp is the narrowest carry the pair has offered in years and is contracting from both ends, whereas the CAD dossier treats CAD/JPY as its cleanest bullish-CAD expression; the 10-year GoC–JGB spread has compressed roughly 120bp over twelve months while the pair rose 1.91%, which means the pair has banked none of the differential compression and carries all of the catch-up risk; and both legs are at speculative short extremes versus the dollar, which mutes the pair-level positioning signal that either dossier reads as a squeeze setup. We are tactically Bearish CAD/JPY with conviction 3 (weighted score −0.2494) targeting 110.00, and strategically Bearish with conviction 2 (score −0.1438) targeting 107.50. The caveat is material and dated: if Brent holds above $95 and the BoJ fails to hike on 18 September, the terms-of-trade and fiscal channels — the two largest positive contributors in this analysis — reassert and the 114.42–114.82 moving-average cluster becomes the target instead.

market_context.valuation_assessment: The two dossiers disagree on pair-level fair value and the disagreement is methodological, not empirical. The CAD dossier's relative-REER approach, dividing Canada's BIS real broad index of 95.71 by Japan's 65.30, produces an implied CAD/JPY of 77.15 and a headline claim that the yen is 46.57% cheap — a level-ratio calculation that is not a valuation anchor because BIS indices are not comparable across countries in levels. The JPY dossier's deviation-from-own-mean approach is the defensible one: with the yen 7.82% below its 30-month mean and the Canadian dollar 2.84% below its own, the yen is roughly 5.0% cheap to the Canadian dollar, implying a fair value of 107.42 against spot of 111.99 — the pair is approximately 4.3% rich. We use the second figure and flag the first as unusable. Japan's real broad effective exchange rate at 65.30 is the lowest reading ever recorded for the currency on the BIS measure, while Canada's 95.71 sits near the tenth percentile of its own history. Both currencies are cheap; the yen is cheap at a multi-decade extreme and the Canadian dollar is cheap at a cyclical one. Over a multi-year horizon that asymmetry pulls CAD/JPY lower. What is priced at 111.99 is a world in which Japan's real undervaluation is permanent and Canada's is cyclical — precisely the assumption the July intervention and the BoJ's stated 2% neutral rate are designed to break.

market_context.recent_regime: Through the first three weeks of July the pair was in a low-volatility grind higher, advancing from 113.6 on 3 July to 116.47 on 23 July on the twin engines of a 31% Brent rally and a yen sliding toward a 40-year low. That regime ended in two sessions: the 30 July intervention produced a 3.71-yen daily range and the largest single-day decline in the pair in years, and the subsequent four sessions have consolidated in a tight 110.77-113.03 band rather than retracing, which is the behaviour of a market that has genuinely repriced rather than merely gapped. The dominant narrative for the next month is whether coordinated official action plus a hawkish BoJ can convert a squeeze into a trend, against a Canadian dollar that has an unpriced 50% tariff cliff arriving on 19 August.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: The Bank of Canada's overnight rate target of 2.25% against the Bank of Japan's 1.00% gives CAD/JPY an annualised carry of +125bp in favour of a long-pair position, equal to 1.40 yen per year or 11.7 pips per month. Against an estimated 3M implied volatility of 10%, the carry-to-vol ratio is approximately 0.13 — the thinnest of any high-differential yen cross (AUD/JPY 335bp at ~0.35, NOK/JPY 325bp at ~0.31, GBP/JPY 275bp at ~0.34). The carry regime worked through 23 July but has since failed in real time: the pair fell 4.48 yen from the 23 July high, destroying roughly 38 months of accrued carry in five sessions. Because the differential is so narrow, the forward market finances away almost none of a bearish view — the six-month forward implies only 0.62% depreciation, meaning the entire expected move is genuine edge, which is the structural reason CAD/JPY is a more capital-efficient short than AUD/JPY despite being a less crowded one.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The differential is +125bp at the policy rate, +135.3bp at the two-year (GoC 2.85% versus JGB 1.497%) and only +78.9bp at the ten-year (GoC 3.59% versus JGB 2.801%), and every one of those spreads is narrower than a year ago. The trajectory is the whole story: over twelve months the ten-year JGB rose roughly 122bp while the Government of Canada ten-year barely moved, compressing the pair's long-end spread from roughly 200bp to 79bp — and CAD/JPY rose 1.91% over the same period. The pair has therefore banked precisely none of a 120bp compression in its own primary driver, which means the accumulated mispricing sits entirely on the downside. Inside four weeks neither central bank meets, so the differential is a fixed parameter, but the distribution of surprise around it is one-sided: the BoC's own Market Participants Survey has 2.25% held through December with no hike until March 2027, so Canada's leg cannot narrow the gap, while public sources price the 18 September BoJ meeting somewhere between 16% and 35% for a 25bp move against a board that has stated neutral is 'around 2 percent' and a Governor who said on 31 July there is a chance the Bank could speed up the pace of hikes. The transmission is direct: because CAD/JPY's carry is only 125bp, a single 25bp BoJ hike removes a fifth of the pair's entire yield support, whereas the same hike removes only 7% of AUD/JPY's. Two dated events inside the window can move September pricing — the BoJ Summary of Opinions on 10 August and Japan's July national CPI on 20 August, which follows a Tokyo July core print of 1.9% against a 1.7% consensus.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the gap-to-neutral asymmetry dominates and it is stark. The BoJ's policy rate of 1.00% sits roughly 100bp below its own board's stated neutral of around 2%, the largest such gap in the G10; the BoC's 2.25% sits 50bp below its own 2.75% neutral estimate. Japan therefore has twice the latent tightening capacity, and its constraint is loosening while Canada's is tightening: Japanese core-core is forecast at 2.5% for FY2026 and 2.6% for FY2027 with CPI risks officially skewed to the upside, whereas Canadian CPI-trim at 1.80% and CPI-median at 1.90% are both below target and falling, giving Governing Council mandate cover to remain anchored. Our expectation is BoJ at 1.50% by end-Q1 2027 against a BoC that reaches at most 2.50% on the oil-driven hawkish scenario the CAD dossier identifies for the 28 October MPR — a differential of 75–100bp versus roughly 104bp priced, and versus 175bp a year ago. Mechanically, a 50bp compression in a 125bp differential is a 40% reduction in the pair's carry support, and pairs whose carry halves do not hold their level. The counterweight, which keeps confidence at 60 rather than higher, is the disconfirming evidence itself: 120bp of compression has already been delivered without the pair falling, because the rise in Japanese yields has been a fiscal risk premium concentrated in the super-long rather than a policy premium in the front end. The observable resolution test is whether the next leg of JGB repricing is led by the two-year or the thirty-year.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The growth differential and the inflation differential point in opposite directions with almost equal force, which is a genuine offset rather than an absence of information. On growth, Canada has the stronger impulse: real GDP inflected from 0.0% quarter-on-quarter in Q1 to roughly +0.8% in Q2, unemployment fell for a second consecutive month to 6.5%, wages accelerated to 3.3% and retail sales hit a record — against Japan's Q1 +0.45% quarter-on-quarter and a consensus of roughly +0.80% annualised for Q2. On inflation, Japan has the stronger impulse and it is the one that matters for policy: Tokyo July core printed 1.9% against a 1.7% consensus with core-core at 2.0%, domestic corporate goods prices are running at 7.1% year-on-year with yen-based import prices at 29.7%, while Canada's BoC-preferred cores fell to 1.80% trim and 1.90% median, both below target. The bilateral transmission is asymmetric in a way neither dossier captures: Canadian growth beats do not move CAD/JPY much because they do not change the BoC's reaction function while core inflation is below target, whereas Japanese inflation beats move the pair directly because they change the probability of a September hike that is only 16-35% priced. That asymmetry means the pair is more sensitive to the 20 August Japanese CPI than to the 28 August Canadian GDP print, despite the latter being the larger number. Event clustering is dense: Canada's Labour Force Survey on 7 August, Japan's Summary of Opinions on 10 August, Canadian CPI on 17 August, Japanese trade on 19 August, Japanese CPI on 20 August, Canadian Q2 GDP on 28 August.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the inflation differential dominates the growth differential because policy, not activity, is what reprices exchange rates over quarters. Japan's inflation-expectations regime has demonstrably shifted — Tankan corporate expectations of 2.7% at one year and 2.6% at three and five years, all above target and all higher than March, and a household survey in which 90.4% expect higher prices, the highest since the series began in 2006 — while Canada's has not, with the BoC projecting core back at 2.0% by Q4-2026 and headline at 2.4%. Growth converges rather than diverges: the BoC projects Canadian growth of just 0.7% in 2026 against potential of 1.1%, while the BoJ projects 0.6% for FY2026 against potential of 0.5-1.0%, so both economies run at or slightly below potential and neither generates a growth-driven currency case. The bilateral implication is that the inflation gap does the work: an economy with above-target inflation expectations and a policy rate 100bp below neutral will tighten, and an economy with below-target core and a policy rate 50bp below neutral will not — which compresses the differential and pulls the pair down. The offsetting risk, and the reason confidence is only 52, is that Japan's inflation impulse is imported: goods PPI at 7.1% against core-core at 1.7% is a 5.4-point wedge, and if the energy shock reverses, the Japanese inflation case reverses with it — while Canada's oil-driven upside inflation risk would reverse simultaneously, leaving the differential broadly unchanged.

Over four weeks the level of activity matters and Canada's is improving faster, offsetting Japan's inflation momentum. The weight halves from 0.18 to 0.10, which limits the contribution change to roughly 0.05.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: CAD/JPY is a moderate risk-sensitivity cross, not a pure risk proxy, and the current regime classification matters. The framework places CAD/JPY alongside EUR/JPY and GBP/JPY in the moderate band rather than with AUD/JPY and NZD/JPY in the high-beta band, because the Canadian dollar's own equity beta is dampened by its US trade linkage — roughly 75% of Canadian goods exports go to the United States, so a strong US economy supports the Canadian dollar through the trade channel even when it hurts it through the rate channel. The environment is unambiguously risk-on: VIX at 17.09, US investment-grade spreads at 0.80% and high yield at 2.84% near cycle tights, the S&P 500 at 7,489.72 and the Nikkei at 64,362. On a straight reading that is pair-positive, because the yen is the G10's most VIX-negative currency and the Canadian dollar is a commodity proxy. But the 30 July session demonstrated the offsetting mechanism live: CAD/JPY fell 2.12% on a day when the VIX did not spike, which means the transmission was positioning and official flow, not risk aversion. That is the crux of the Neutral: risk appetite is currently supporting the pair through the equity channel while simultaneously being the precondition for the carry unwind that is destroying it. Cross-asset signals specific to this pair run the same way — Brent at $91.82 is pair-positive through the Canadian leg and pair-negative through the Japanese import bill, so the commodity-risk complex does not resolve the direction either.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months the asymmetry replaces the level and it runs against the pair. Yen realised volatility percentiles were in the bottom decile on three tenors simultaneously before the intervention, credit spreads sit within 46bp of their all-time low, and distributions that compressed mean-revert upward far more often than downward — and the pair's convexity to that reversion is negative, because the yen is the funding leg. The bilateral mechanism is specific: a volatility regime shift forces simultaneous covering of a 185,047-contract yen short while the Canadian dollar's own 203,655-contract short is also covered, but the yen covering is larger in cross terms because the yen short is held against higher-beta currencies. The volatility premium raises the cost of holding carry trades and erodes the yield differential that made them attractive, a differential that in CAD/JPY's case is only 125bp and therefore the first to become uneconomic. The counterweight is that the Canadian dollar is not a high-beta risk currency and would outperform the Australian and New Zealand dollars in a risk-off episode, so CAD/JPY would fall less than AUD/JPY. There is also a genuine two-sided tail: a Strait of Hormuz resolution would be risk-positive globally but would collapse oil, hurting the Canadian leg while helping the Japanese one — which is pair-negative through a different channel and reinforces the bearish read rather than offsetting it. For CAD/JPY, escalation and resolution are both ambiguous-to-negative, because escalation raises oil (pair-positive) but triggers risk-off (pair-negative), while resolution lowers oil (pair-negative) and lifts risk (pair-positive) — but the second-round effect on Japan's terms of trade in the resolution case is larger than the first-round effect on Canadian export receipts.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both legs are short against the dollar at percentile extremes, which mutes the pair-level signal — and the muting is itself the finding. Canadian dollar net specs sit at approximately the 99th percentile short with leveraged funds at −102,495 contracts and asset managers at −101,160; yen positioning sits at the 4th percentile with a combined −185,047 as of the 28 July report. In cross terms those largely cancel, so CAD/JPY is not a crowded long the way AUD/JPY is, and there is no pair-specific carry-trade community to squeeze. What breaks the tie is timing and mechanism. The yen squeeze catalyst has fired: in just two days at the end of last week, authorities reversed more than two months of losses in the yen, using direct purchases, calls to banks that deal in the currency, and jawboning. The Canadian dollar squeeze catalyst has not — and the one dated Canadian catalyst inside the window, the Section 338 tariff effective date around 19 August, points against the Canadian dollar rather than toward a squeeze. So the covering flow reaching CAD/JPY through the yen leg is currently unopposed. There is a further bilateral flow dynamic: Japanese investors turned away from Canadian bonds in early 2022, partly due to costlier FX hedging costs, with net flows from Japan into Canadian bonds negative in 16 of 19 months and Japan's relative share of Canadian bond holdings driven to a four-decade low — a dated observation, but one that establishes that the structural Japan-to-Canada portfolio bid which historically supported CAD/JPY is largely absent, so the pair lacks the bilateral flow floor that AUD/JPY has from Japanese retail and Uridashi demand.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months both positioning extremes normalise and the pair-level signal genuinely disappears. The Canadian dollar short is funded at 137.5bp against the dollar and has already survived a 31% Brent rally without covering, so it is rational and durable; the yen short is funded at 262.5bp and has twice rebuilt after intervention, with traders already bidding puts on the yen as intervention picked up, the first indication that short positions are being rebuilt. What replaces positioning is the structural flow balance, and for this pair it is finely poised. On the yen-negative side, GPIF's announced seven-point rotation out of JGBs into foreign equities is roughly USD 52bn of structural yen selling. On the yen-positive side, none of Japan's ten major life insurers plans to increase unhedged foreign bonds, four intend to add JGBs, and the group's FY2026 term-end planning assumption is USD/JPY 154 — a standing bid that activates on yen weakness. On the Canadian side, Canadian pension funds' foreign-asset hedging generates persistent two-way Canadian dollar flow that dwarfs futures positioning and is invisible in the COT data. Bilaterally, the decisive structural point is that with the GoC-JGB ten-year spread down to 79bp, the yield case for a Japanese institution to hold hedged Canadian duration has all but vanished — 79bp does not survive a hedging cost, capping any recovery in the Japan-to-Canada bond bid that would otherwise support the pair.

This is the key insight neither dossier can make on its own.

That is the scenario we assign 25% to and it is why strategic conviction is 2 rather than 3.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the pair's strongest positive and the reason the bearish call is conviction 3 rather than 4. The terms-of-trade differential is extreme and widening: Canada's terms-of-trade index stood at 107.5 in Q1-2026 while Japan's collapsed to 83.95 in May from 88.34 in April, a 5.0% single-month deterioration against a since-1960 average of 150.50. The mechanism is one commodity acting twice. Brent rose from $70.16 on 26 June to $91.82 on 27 July, peaking intramonth at $105.32 on 23 July, and on the framework's direction rules oil up is strongly positive for Canada and strongly negative for Japan — the only combination in the rulebook that is doubly positive for a single pair. Japan's June mineral fuel imports were JPY 2.10tn, up 41.9% year-on-year, with petroleum import values up 59.3% while crude oil import volumes fell 13.7%, producing a second consecutive monthly trade deficit of JPY 406.9bn against a JPY 120bn consensus. Canada, over the same window, printed a record $77.1bn monthly export month and its largest bilateral surplus with the United States since January 2025. JKM LNG at $21.33/mmBtu compounds the Japanese side. Bilateral trade itself is a minor channel: per IMF DOTS, Canada exported $10.9bn of goods to Japan and imported $16.2bn in 2024, a net Canadian goods deficit of $5.2bn, with total bilateral goods trade of roughly $27bn, less than half a single month of Canadian total exports — the direct bilateral trade linkage is structurally trivial; the indirect commodity linkage is dominant. The tactical caveat is that Brent has already fallen 13% from the 23 July spike, and Japan's July trade balance on 19 August should improve for that reason.

That is the largest identifiable mispricing in this analysis and it argues the pair should be higher, not lower.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.19 strategic weight this is the single largest positive contributor and the principal reason strategic conviction is only 2. Terms-of-trade effects are cumulative through the balance of payments rather than sentiment-driven, and over two to three quarters the arithmetic compounds: if Brent holds near current levels, Canada's current account moves from -0.87% of GDP toward balance while Japan's goods deficit widens and its terms of trade approach the 69.80 all-time low of September 2022. The structural asymmetry is close to absolute — Japan imports roughly 99% of its oil, and a weaker yen amplifies the local-currency cost, which is the feedback loop that has driven yen-based import prices up 29.7% year-on-year. Japan's supply reshuffling — June LNG from Russia up 52% and from the United States up 51% while Middle East volumes collapsed from 356kt to 126kt — mitigates security of supply but costs money. The structural offsets are genuine: Canadian egress is capped, with Trans Mountain at 85% average utilisation and the Enbridge Mainline at 95.2%, so Canada monetises price but not volume; the WTI-WCS discount is assumed roughly $15 wide; and the Section 338 tariffs hit approximately $20bn of Canadian exports. And the oil path itself is contested — the EIA's July outlook forecasts Brent at $74 in Q3-2026 and $65 in 2027, while the BoJ's own July Outlook assumes Dubai falling from $80 to $70. If that path realises, this factor reverses and the strategic bearish case becomes materially stronger.

That is a one-sided pricing of a two-sided situation and it means the bearish pair thesis carries positive convexity risk against it.

factors.horizon_split: Both horizons are Bullish with strategic confidence (64) above tactical (60), the inverse of the usual pattern and deliberately so. A 31% oil move changes almost nothing about Canadian export receipts or Japanese import bills inside four weeks, but changes both materially over two quarters — which is why the weight rises from 0.09 to 0.19. The strategic confidence premium reflects the completeness of the energy polarity: there is no G10 pair other than NOK/JPY in which one leg's terms-of-trade gain is so nearly the mirror of the other's loss.

Aggregating, the commodity complex is the pair's largest single structural support, though realised sensitivity through July was far below the framework-implied level because Canada's oil beta collapsed to approximately 0.03 (a 31% Brent rally produced only a 1.06% Canadian dollar gain) while the yen leg was captured entirely by intervention and policy.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both central banks have issued conditional hawkish signals, but the BoJ's is more explicit, more recent, and more underpriced — and Japan now has a second, more powerful communication channel that Canada entirely lacks. On the Japanese side, Governor Ueda said on 31 July that if monetary conditions are accommodative there is a chance the Bank could speed up the pace of hikes, that upside price risks must now be the focus, that currency volatility's inflation impact may be larger than in the past, and that the Board will debate policy from the next meeting onward. Takata dissented for an immediate 1.25%. On the Canadian side, the BoC's conditional trigger is real but weaker and slower: Governing Council recorded that a sustained oil increase with broadening spillovers 'would likely require a monetary policy response,' and Macklem said the Bank will not let higher oil become persistent inflation — but Canada has no BoC event before 2 September, and its cores are below target. The bilateral asymmetry is that the BoJ's signal has two publications inside the tactical window while Canada has none at all, so the guidance gap can only close from the Japanese side over four weeks. The second channel is decisive and new: Japan and the US executed a coordinated intervention in late July 2026, the first of its kind since 2011, and currency strategists are now warning that the rules of the game have quietly changed for speculators. There is no analogous official body publicly committed to defending the Canadian dollar. Credibility differential: the market habitually discounts BoJ hawkishness, which is why September is only 16-35% priced — but coordinated intervention plus a dissenting board member is a harder configuration to discount.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market prices the BoC as fully neutral through December and applies a historical credibility discount to BoJ hawkishness, which is why September sits at 16-35%. We put fair value at 45-50% and note that the coordinated intervention has changed the official reaction function in a way pricing has not reflected — worth 1.0-1.5 yen of downside on repricing alone.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the weight rises to 0.12 and the question becomes which bank's stated framework the market will be forced to believe. Both have dated reckonings: the BoC's 28 October MPR must revise an oil assumption built on the 9 July futures curve ($65 WTI, $75 Brent) against an $84 market, and the BoJ's 30 October Outlook Report must show whether FY2027 core rises above the current 2.4% as energy subsidies roll off. The bilateral asymmetry is in the size of the required revision relative to the size of the gap to neutral: the BoC's hawkish revision buys it perhaps 25bp toward a 2.75% neutral it is 50bp below, while the BoJ's buys it a path toward a 2% neutral it is 100bp below. On credibility, the picture is genuinely mixed and confidence is capped at 58 accordingly. The BoC is the more transparent and historically reliable communicator; the BoJ is the G10's most opaque by construction, faces a politically expansionary Takaichi government with a 352-seat supermajority whose Cabinet Office representative asked the Bank to act 'while understanding initiatives taken by the Takaichi Cabinet,' and held when it could have hiked into a 40-year low. Against that, Japan's official reaction function now has external validation: the US Treasury's 23 July report described substantial yen undervaluation and said normalisation would help anchor inflation expectations, and Goldman Sachs strategists wrote that authorities would likely intervene further in coming days if the yen begins to unwind the recent move, and that intervention is an effective tool to buy time before fundamental factors turn more positive.

The bilateral edge is that the BoJ's underpricing is larger in absolute terms than the BoC's, and that Japan alone has an official body actively defending its currency.

Tactically the case rests on event density — three BoJ publications against zero BoC events — plus the coordinated intervention's standing threat. Strategically it rests on the relative size of each bank's gap to its own neutral rate and on whether the BoJ's credibility discount survives a 30 October Outlook Report that must confront energy-subsidy roll-off. The weight nearly doubles from 0.07 to 0.12, so the contribution rises from -0.0406 to -0.0696 without any change of view.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: CAD/JPY faces the unusual configuration of adverse dated event risk on both legs inside the same four-week window, which is why this factor is a confident Bearish rather than the Neutral either dossier's standalone geopolitical read would suggest. On the Canadian leg, three presidential proclamations signed 20 July impose 50% Section 338 tariffs on Canadian motor vehicles, alcoholic beverages and dairy covering approximately $20bn of exports, effective around 19 August, applying regardless of USMCA origin after the United States declined on 1 July to renew the agreement — a Canada-specific negative with no Japanese equivalent. On the Japanese leg, the intervention risk is now a standing constraint on pair upside rather than a tail: while many question authorities' capacity to change the yen's long-term trajectory in a $9.5 trillion-per-day market, there is no doubt of their power in short bursts, and in two days they reversed more than two months of losses. Both legs' event risks therefore point the pair down. The one event that points up is energy escalation, and its transmission for this pair is genuinely doubly positive — a Hormuz re-closure raises Canadian export prices and Japanese import costs simultaneously. But that channel has empirically failed twice in 2026: the mid-July escalation drove Brent above $100 and CAD/JPY made no new high beyond 116.47, because the yen's safe-haven bid and Japan's terms-of-trade hit offset while Canada's oil beta collapsed to near zero.

tactical.what_is_priced: The pair moved barely at all on the 20 July tariff proclamation, implying the market assumes deferral or dilution, and the option surface prices essentially no premium for the 19 August date. Neither leg's dated event risk is in the price, and three of the four dated events point the same way.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months the distribution widens on both legs and confidence falls accordingly, but the direction holds. On the Canadian side the USMCA renewal question is now open-ended, which converts a discrete event into a persistent risk premium for an economy sending roughly 75% of its goods exports to a single partner — and the 2025-26 precedent of tariff reversal (IEEPA tariffs terminated by executive order in February 2026) makes a negotiated withdrawal a live, pair-positive branch worth perhaps 25%. On the Japanese side the strategic event set is more concentrated and more pair-bearish: three BoJ meetings, an Outlook Report, the FY2027 budget and JGB issuance plan in late December, and a demonstrated willingness to intervene repeatedly. The bilateral novelty is that Washington's participation has changed the geopolitics of yen weakness: concerns in Washington over the risks posed by sharp yen depreciation and rising JGB volatility, particularly potential spillover to the US Treasury market, appear to be part of the backdrop, and the more the yen's depreciation gives Japan a trade advantage over the US, the more it is likely to irk Trump. That means further yen weakness now carries a political cost to Japan in its most important trade relationship, a constraint that did not exist three months ago and that has no Canadian analogue. Set against it, the $150 billion spent since 2022 shows Japan's commitment is real but has not produced a lasting trend reversal.

factors.horizon_split: Both horizons are Bearish with confidence stepping down from 60 to 52. The tactical case is two hard dates on opposite legs pointing the same way within one week; the strategic case is the same instruments viewed through a longer lens in which the Canadian tariff branch has a credible reversal path while the Japanese intervention constraint becomes structural rather than episodic. The weight is constant at 0.05, so the confidence decay is the only contribution change.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: The fiscal differential is not background for this pair — Japan's fiscal risk premium is the identified mechanism by which the pair rose despite 120bp of yield-spread compression, and it is therefore load-bearing rather than immaterial

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The fiscal differential is one of the widest in the G10 and, unusually, its tactical sign has just inverted. Canada carries federal debt of 41.2% of GDP with ratings of Aaa from Moody's, AAA from S&P and DBRS and AA+ from Fitch, all stable, deficits of 1.9-2.1% of GDP, and a ten-year yield of 3.59% that is the lowest in the commodity G10. Japan carries consolidated central-plus-local debt of 187.6% of GDP, ratings of A1/A+/A, a record JPY 122.3tn FY2026 budget with debt service up 10.8% on a 3.0% interest assumption that is a 29-year high, and a 30-year JGB at 3.971% within 4bp of its all-time high. That is a four-to-five notch rating gap and a 146-point debt-ratio gap, and on the conventional reading it is emphatically pair-positive: a fiscally deteriorating quote currency should depreciate. Through 2026 it did exactly that — the mechanism by which Japanese yields rose without the yen benefiting was a fiscal risk premium concentrated in the super-long, and that is what carried CAD/JPY from 105 to 117. The inversion is that the same risk premium has now triggered official action rather than currency weakness, because JGB volatility has become a US Treasury market problem and thus a reason for Washington to help buy yen. That leaves the factor genuinely two-sided over four weeks: worse Japanese fiscal news now raises both the yen risk premium and the probability of further intervention.

tactical.what_is_priced: The JGB curve prices Japan's fiscal risk honestly at a 30-year of 3.971%; the pair has priced it as a permanent yen discount. Tactically there is no edge, because any further deterioration now produces two offsetting responses — a wider risk premium and a higher intervention probability.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the fiscal differential reasserts as a pair-positive because the compounding is one-directional. Japan is refinancing a 187.6%-of-GDP debt stock at progressively higher coupons every quarter while the BoJ shrinks its holdings from roughly JPY 518tn to a projected JPY 480tn by end-March 2027, and a board member has publicly warned that halting the taper risks purchases being perceived as fiscal financing. Canada is refinancing a 41.2% stock at 3.59% against projected trend growth of 1.8%, which is a stable-to-improving debt dynamic, and has ample fiscal space to respond to the tariff shock without threatening its credit. The bilateral transmission for the pair is that a fiscal risk premium in the quote currency is a persistent structural bid for the base currency, and this one has 146 points of debt ratio and four notches of rating behind it. This is the factor that best explains the pair's twelve-month resilience and the reason the strategic bearish score is only -0.1438 rather than -0.20. The constraints are real: roughly 90% of JGBs are domestically held, ratings are stable with no agency action, Japan's record current account surplus finances the state internally, and the FY2026 issuance plan actually cut calendar-base market issuance by JPY 3.8tn. This is slow erosion, not crisis — but slow erosion in a 187.6% debt ratio against a AAA counterpart is a durable pair-positive.

strategic.what_is_priced: The pair has priced Japan's fiscal position as a permanent structural discount and Canada's as unremarkable, which is broadly correct. The strategic edge is small and directional: Japan's flow picture is improving even as its stock deteriorates, so the fiscal contribution is a persistent one-to-two-yen support rather than an accelerating one — unless the 30-year breaks 4.25%.

factors.horizon_split: The stance moves from Neutral to Bullish because the tactical inversion — Japanese fiscal stress triggering coordinated intervention — operates within days, while the compounding refinancing arithmetic operates over quarters. Over four weeks the intervention response dominates and cancels the risk premium; over six months the risk premium accumulates faster than any single intervention can offset, which is why the weight rises from 0.05 to 0.09.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The pair's own chart has broken decisively and the volatility surface has not caught up. Spot at 111.99 is below the 50-day SMA at 114.42254, the 100-day at 114.82217 and the 200-day at 114.81054, having broken all three within five sessions; the 50-day has crossed marginally below the 200-day while the 100-day and 200-day sit 0.012 yen apart. That is a freshly inverted rather than an exhausted downtrend, so trend-following flow has only just flipped to selling the pair. Realised volatility computed from the daily closes has exploded from roughly 4.5-5% in mid-July to approximately 13.6% across the seven sessions spanning the intervention, with a 3.71-yen single-day range on 30 July against 0.3-0.5 yen ranges a fortnight earlier. Against an estimated 1M implied of 11-12%, realised is running above implied, which favours spot expression over long options for a directional view. The skew is the pair-specific tell and it runs against consensus: with yen puts bid by more than four vols over yen calls, the CAD/JPY topside wing is expensive and the downside wing is comparatively cheap, so the market is paying up for exactly the outcome we expect not to happen. Levels are dense immediately below spot — 111.85 is 14 pips away and 110.77 is the 3 August low — which means the pair sits on a knife-edge where a single close below 111.85 opens 110.00 quickly. Liquidity is a genuine consideration: CAD/JPY is a second-tier cross with Asian-session gap risk, and the 30 July range proves it.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the structure is unresolved and forcing a stance would be noise at a 0.03 weight. The pair remains at the 57th percentile of a 52-week range that runs from 104.786 to 117.49155, so it has retraced to the middle of its range rather than broken it, and the multi-year advance from the June 2025 low at 104.786 is technically intact until the pair establishes a sustained monthly close below roughly 110.00 — which would confirm a lower high at 117.49 and a lower low. The moving-average complex is converged rather than fanned: 100d and 200d within 0.012 yen means the long-term trend is flat, not down, and it would take several months of sustained lower prices to produce a decisive bearish alignment. That is the honest counterweight to the tactical break. On volatility, the strategic reading is that volatility explodes on impact then fades as traders regroup and reassess positioning, but just because volatility diminishes does not mean there is no impact, as intervention usually preceded turning points — so we expect the pair's implied volatility to settle back toward 8-9% while the directional consequence persists. Round-number interest at 110.00 and 115.00 will act as magnets, and 110.00 in particular is likely to carry barrier concentration given its proximity to the November 2025 base.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Dollar funding conditions are ample and untroubled — SOFR at 3.65% exactly at interest on reserve balances, effective fed funds at 3.63%, a Federal Reserve balance sheet of $6,738.19bn that is expanding rather than shrinking after the end of QT, no swap-line usage, and a broad dollar index at 120.71 — and for a cross like CAD/JPY that benign backdrop has little directional content. The mechanism through which USD conditions reach this pair is the vehicle-currency channel: most CAD/JPY flow settles through the dollar, so a softer dollar lifts both legs and a firmer dollar depresses both, netting close to zero. The bilateral asymmetry that would matter is the cross-currency basis differential, and here the evidence is one-sided in an unhelpful way: the Canadian dollar's USD basis is habitually among the tightest in the complex given the depth of Canada-US banking integration, while the JPY/USD basis is the single most important funding variable for the quote leg and was not retrievable this cycle — a gap flagged in both dossiers and the principal reason confidence is capped at 45. What can be observed is that a widening negative JPY/USD basis would raise the cost for Japanese institutions to hold hedged foreign assets and trigger repatriation, which is pair-bearish; and that with the GoC-JGB ten-year spread at only 79bp, Canadian duration is already uneconomic for a hedged Japanese buyer, so the pair has no basis-driven support to lose.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the end of quantitative tightening and the Desk's shift to purchasing Treasury bills constitute a structural loosening of global dollar supply that historically weighs on the dollar with a lag of two to four quarters. For a USD pair that would be a first-order signal; for CAD/JPY it is close to second-order, because a weaker dollar lifts both the Canadian dollar and the yen and the net cross effect depends on relative betas rather than on the dollar itself. The one dated, directional item inside the strategic window is the 31 December year-end funding turn, which reliably widens cross-currency basis and produces a temporary dollar bid — historically a mild pair-positive, because the yen leg is the more heavily hedged of the two and Japanese institutions' year-end hedge rollovers dominate the flow. The offsetting strategic consideration is the repatriation channel: if the JPY/USD basis widens materially, Japanese institutions reduce foreign-asset exposure and buy yen, which is pair-bearish and would compound the carry-unwind mechanism. Because we cannot measure the basis, we cannot rank these channels, and Neutral at 45 is the honest score. The weight reduction from 0.12 to 0.07 reflects that this is a cross, not that the factor is unimportant.

tactical.score_interpretation: A net score of -0.2494 on a -1.00 to +1.00 scale is a solidly bearish reading for the pair. One factor, Policy & Rates, contributes -0.1488, and it takes the entire terms-of-trade contribution of +0.0540 plus nothing else on the positive side to offset even a third of it, while four separate bearish factors — Flows, Guidance, Event Risk and Market Structure — add a further -0.1546. Three factors carrying 30% of the tactical weight contribute exactly zero, reflecting genuine two-sidedness rather than analytical laziness.
tactical.rationale: At tactical weights the pair's problem is that its yield support is both the thinnest and the fastest-eroding of any yen cross. Policy & Rates carries 0.24, the largest weight in the framework, and it is unambiguously bearish for CAD/JPY: a +125bp differential is the narrowest carry among yen crosses that offer meaningful differential, and it has already contracted by roughly 50bp over twelve months at the policy level and by 120bp at the ten-year, while the pair rose 1.91% over the same period — meaning none of the compression already delivered has been banked and all of the catch-up risk sits on the downside. Neither central bank meets inside the window, so the differential is fixed, but the surprise distribution is one-sided: Canada cannot narrow the gap because its cores are below target and its own survey has 2.25% held through December, while the BoJ has three dated publications inside the window and a September meeting priced at only 16-35% against a Governor who has said the Bank could speed up the pace of hikes. Against that sits the single genuinely powerful bull argument, and it is the factor the standalone dossiers most disagree about: the pair's terms-of-trade differential is the most extreme in the G10 outside NOK/JPY, with Canada at 107.5 and Japan at 83.95 after a 5.0% single-month collapse, and with Brent up 31% acting doubly — positively on the Canadian leg and negatively on the Japanese import bill of JPY 2.10tn, up 41.9% year-on-year. The base and quote dossier views conflict on the surface but reinforce beneath it: the CAD dossier's own admission that Canada's oil beta collapsed to 0.03 is precisely why the terms-of-trade tailwind has not reached CAD/JPY, and the JPY dossier's conviction 4 tactical bullish yen call is precisely what has been driving the pair. Three bilateral-specific factors modify the standalone views decisively. First, positioning is offsetting at the pair level — a 99th-percentile short Canadian dollar against a 4th-percentile short yen means CAD/JPY is not a crowded trade, so it lacks both AUD/JPY's squeeze fuel and its crowding risk; what remains is asymmetric timing, with the yen squeeze catalyst fired and the Canadian one dated 19 August and pointing the wrong way. Second, the intervention is coordinated with the US Treasury for the first time since 2011, creating an official constraint on pair upside with no Canadian counterpart. Third, the pair's own chart has broken all three moving averages in five sessions with realised volatility above implied. What is priced versus what we expect: the market prices a failed intervention, a resumption of the July uptrend, and a BoJ that stays put — the skew is bid for pair upside and spot is holding just above 111.85. We expect 111.85 to give way, the 10 August Summary of Opinions to lift September pricing toward 45%, and the 19 August tariffs to hit the base leg in the same week the 20 August Japanese CPI hits the quote leg. The path of least resistance is lower, bounded by 111.85 and 110.77 below and by 113.30 and 113.96 above. Catalysts are dense and dated across early through late August. Conviction is 3 rather than 4 because the terms-of-trade factor is the highest-confidence bullish input in the analysis and because we are trading against a documented option skew; conviction is 3 rather than 2 because four independent bearish factors point the same way and the pair's carry cushion of 11.7 pips a month provides essentially no protection.
tactical.g10_relative_ranking: Among the eight liquid yen crosses, CAD/JPY ranks 4th most attractive as a short — behind AUD/JPY (335bp of carry to unwind, the widest valuation gap, the most crowded positioning), behind NZD/JPY (150bp with an RBNZ hiking into 4.1% inflation), and behind GBP/JPY (275bp of carry against a Bank of England on hold). It ranks ahead of EUR/JPY, where a September ECB hike widens the gap before it narrows, and well ahead of NOK/JPY, which is the wrong side of the same energy trade. Among Canadian dollar crosses, CAD/JPY ranks 2nd among bearish-CAD expressions, behind short CAD/NOK, where Norway pays 200bp more carry to own the identical oil shock with no WCS discount, no egress cap and no Section 338 exposure. CAD/JPY is directly opposed to the CAD dossier's own recommendation of long CAD/JPY as its cleanest bullish expression; we disagree on the carry being eroding rather than durable, the oil asymmetry having failed to transmit given Canada's collapsed oil beta, and the quote leg's new coordinated official support.

tactical.path_expectation: We expect a three-phase, retrace-then-resume shape rather than a straight line. Phase one, roughly 6-12 August, should see a counter-rally toward 113.30 and possibly 113.96 as the official bid withdraws and carry accounts re-engage — this is the modal post-intervention pattern, and volatility has historically been significantly lower after the initial shock, allowing the yen to drift weaker and yen pairs to recover much of their intervention-related losses. That bounce will feel like a failure of the thesis and should be treated as normal. Phase two, roughly 12-21 August, is where the move is decided: the 10 August Summary of Opinions and the 20 August Japanese CPI hit the quote leg while the 19 August tariff date hits the base leg, and our base case is that the alignment breaks 111.85 and delivers 110.00 with the character of a stair-step rather than a spike, because the forced covering has already occurred and what follows is discretionary repositioning. Phase three, the final week, should see consolidation in the 109.50-111.00 zone as attention rotates to Canadian Q2 GDP on 28 August and the 2 September BoC meeting. Volatility should stay elevated relative to the 4.5-5% mid-July reading, plausibly settling at 9-11%, with the widest daily ranges around 19-20 August; expect at least one 150-pip counter-rally that tests conviction. Pullback resistance on any decline is 113.30 then 113.96; support on any further break is 110.77 then 110.00. The single most likely way this expectation is wrong is that the tariffs are deferred in the days before 19 August, which would collapse phase two entirely and turn the month into a squeeze of the Canadian leg.

strategic.score_interpretation: At -0.1438 the strategic score clears the neutral band but only just, and the mechanism of the reduction from the tactical -0.2494 lies almost entirely in weights rather than in stances. External Balance rises from 0.09 to 0.19, taking its contribution from +0.0540 to +0.1216, and Fiscal rises from 0.05 to 0.09 while flipping to Bullish, contributing +0.0522 where it contributed zero tactically. Those two changes add +0.120 to the score. Offsetting them, Inflation & Growth and Risk Appetite both turn Bearish and Guidance's weight nearly doubles its contribution, while the tactical Flows and Market Structure contributions disappear entirely. Over six months the framework stops paying for the squeeze and the broken chart, and starts paying for the balance of payments and the sovereign credit — both of which support the pair.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the case against CAD/JPY rests on rates and guidance, and the case for it rests on terms of trade and sovereign credit — and the second pair is nearly as large as the first, which is why conviction is 2. Policy & Rates remains the largest weight at 0.24 and remains bearish at -0.1440, because the gap-to-neutral asymmetry is stark: the BoJ sits roughly 100bp below its own board's 2% neutral estimate while the BoC sits 50bp below its 2.75%, so Japan has double the latent tightening capacity and its inflation constraint is loosening while Canada's is binding. Our expectation of a 75-100bp differential by Q1-2027 against roughly 104bp priced is worth 25-50bp of compression in a differential that starts at only 125bp — a 20-40% reduction in the pair's entire carry support. Guidance & Credibility at 0.12 reinforces it: the BoJ's underpricing is larger in absolute terms than the BoC's, and Japan alone has an official body actively defending its currency, now with US participation for the first time since 2011. Against that stands the strongest structural bull case in this cycle's cross set. The terms-of-trade differential at a 0.19 weight is the second-heaviest factor in the framework and it is the most complete energy polarity in the G10 outside NOK/JPY: Canada exports a record 4.3 MMb/d while Japan imports roughly 99% of its oil, Canada's terms-of-trade index is 107.5 while Japan's is 83.95 and 44% below its long-run average, and Brent up 31% acts doubly in the pair's favour. Fiscal & Sovereign at 0.09 adds a persistent structural bid: a 146-point debt-ratio gap and four notches of rating separation, with a 30-year JGB at 3.971% within 4bp of its all-time high and a Canadian 30-year at 3.99% — essentially identical yields for radically different credits, which is the entire Japanese risk premium in one number and the mechanism by which the pair rose despite 120bp of spread compression. How the base and quote dossier views interact: they conflict on the surface and reinforce beneath it. The CAD dossier's strategic bullish call rests on terms of trade, a cheap real exchange rate and the 28 October MPR; the JPY dossier's rests on the gap to neutral, the intervention regime and a record-cheap real exchange rate. Bilaterally, the terms-of-trade argument favours the pair and the policy argument favours the yen — and the policy argument carries 0.36 of combined weight across Factors 1 and 6 against 0.28 across Factors 5 and 8. What is priced versus what we expect: consensus sits near 115 for Q4-2026, implying the pair rises roughly 3% from spot; we expect it to fall 4%, a divergence of roughly 7-8 yen that rests on our view that the BoJ delivers 50bp rather than 25bp and that the differential compresses toward 75-100bp. The path of least resistance is a range through August and September followed by a decline after the 18 September BoJ meeting. Dated catalysts are the BoJ on 18 September, 30 October and 18 December, the BoC MPR on 28 October and decision on 9 December, and Japan's FY2027 budget and JGB issuance plan in late December. Conviction is 2 rather than 3 because the two structural positives do not decay and because the pair's forward curve, at only 125bp, finances away almost none of the expected move — meaning the entire 4% is genuine edge but also entirely dependent on being directionally right.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically CAD/JPY ranks 5th of eight as a yen-long expression, one place lower than its tactical rank, because the terms-of-trade and fiscal offsets that carry the heaviest strategic weights are stronger in this cross than in any other yen pair except NOK/JPY. It sits behind AUD/JPY, NZD/JPY, GBP/JPY, and EUR/JPY (the euro is a net energy importer like Japan, so the ToT offset that protects CAD/JPY is absent). It sits ahead of only NOK/JPY, CHF/JPY and SGD/JPY among yen crosses. Among Canadian dollar crosses, short CAD/JPY ranks 2nd of nine on a strategic bearish-CAD basis, behind short CAD/NOK, which neutralises the oil variable entirely and captures 200bp more carry. CAD/JPY is the right expression only for someone whose primary conviction is on the yen leg and who wants the cheapest financing cost available among yen crosses, at the price of accepting a terms-of-trade headwind.

strategic.path_expectation: We expect a range-then-inflect shape with a dated turn. Through August and September the tactical forces should give way to consolidation in a 110.00-114.00 band as the intervention effect decays and the market waits for the 18 September BoJ meeting, the single highest-information event in the window; volatility explodes on impact then fades as traders regroup and reassess positioning, and that fade is the mechanism by which the pair recovers into September. The inflection should come at the September or October BoJ meeting — if a hike is delivered, the second phase from October through December is a stair-step decline toward 108.50-109.50, punctuated by two or three counter-rallies of 1.5-2.5 yen, with the 31 December year-end funding turn the most likely source of the largest of them as Japanese hedge rollovers temporarily bid the dollar. The final leg into January delivers 107.50, helped by early anticipation of the March fiscal-year-end repatriation window and by the fading of the Q4 energy-hedging bid that mechanically supports the Canadian dollar in October and November. Volatility should normalise downward toward 8-9% from the current spike, which means the decline should be a grind rather than a series of gaps. Pullback levels on the way down are 110.00, then 108.50, then 107.50; a failure to close below 110.00 on a monthly basis by the December BoJ meeting would be the clearest evidence the thesis is not working. The pattern is best described as a plateau-then-slide: two months of range, then three months of decline.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons are aligned in direction and divergent in magnitude. Seven of ten factor stances are identical or adjacent across horizons; the divergence is generated almost entirely by reweighting rather than by re-analysis. Mechanically, the tactical window is where the pair's broken chart, the fired positioning squeeze and the clustered event risk carry weight, while the strategic window is where the terms-of-trade and sovereign-credit differentials come into their own. The result is that the same view is held less confidently the further out you look, which is the correct shape for a pair whose cyclical drivers are bearish and whose structural drivers are bullish.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The 18 September Bank of Japan meeting, with the 28 October BoC MPR and 30 October BoJ Outlook Report as the confirming pair of events three days apart. A secondary, earlier inflection is the 10 August Summary of Opinions.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Hold the tactical view in size and the strategic view in reduced size, and treat the two as separate positions with separate stops rather than one continuous view. The tactical position should be spot or forward with the downside option wing used opportunistically given the skew, reassessed on 10 August and again on 20 August. The strategic position is better held as a relative-value structure — short CAD/JPY against a smaller long in NOK/JPY — because that pairing neutralises the terms-of-trade factor while retaining the full policy-differential exposure.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Summary of Opinions, 30-31 July meeting
catalysts.rationale: The single highest-information event inside the tactical window and the instrument most likely to close the guidance-versus-pricing gap. It will reveal how many of the eight members who voted to hold did so reluctantly, following Takata's dissent for an immediate 1.25% and Ueda's statement that the Bank could speed up the pace of hikes. Because CAD/JPY's carry is only 125bp, a repricing of September from 25% to 45% removes roughly a fifth of the pair's yield support in a single session.

The July issue was finalised on 1 July before the Hormuz re-escalation and forecast Brent at $74 for Q3-2026 and $65 for 2027, roughly $18 below spot. An upward revision is doubly pair-positive under the framework's direction rules — improving the Canadian export outlook while raising Japan's projected import bill — and would validate the terms-of-trade factor that is the pair's largest structural support at a 0.19 strategic weight.

Genuinely two-sided and pivotal for the differential. June saw CPI-trim fall to 1.80% and CPI-median to 1.90%, both below target — the softest of the cycle. A reversal above 2.0% revives the BoC's hawkish option, widens the differential and is pair-bullish; a further fall toward 1.7% forecloses it for 2026 and is pair-bearish.

catalysts.event: Section 338 tariffs take effect: 50% on Canadian motor vehicles, alcohol and dairy
catalysts.rationale: Three presidential proclamations impose 50% ad valorem duties on approximately $20bn of Canadian exports, applying regardless of USMCA origin after the United States declined on 1 July to renew the agreement, with Canada having announced no retaliation. This is the largest single Canada-specific negative of the year and it has no Japanese analogue, and it lands in the same week as Japan's July CPI, so both legs' catalysts align destructively for the pair.

catalysts.event: Japan July trade balance (MoF customs basis)
catalysts.rationale: June delivered a JPY 406.9bn deficit against a JPY 120bn consensus on record imports, with mineral fuel imports up 41.9% year-on-year. Brent fell 13% between 23 and 27 July, so the July bill should improve, which would remove the most visible live pair-positive datapoint on the terms-of-trade channel and paradoxically weaken the bullish case at the same moment the tariff date weakens the bearish one.

The most important single release in the tactical window for this pair. Tokyo July core printed 1.9% against a 1.7% consensus with core-core at 2.0%, and Tokyo leads the national series by roughly one month, so national core at 1.8% or above against a consensus nearer 1.6% is our central expectation. This print moves the September BoJ probability, and September pricing is the pair's dominant near-term variable given a differential of only 125bp.

Because the intervention was coordinated with the US Treasury, the disclosure also carries information about whether a second tranche was executed.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada interest rate announcement
catalysts.rationale: A hold at 2.25% is close to certain, so the information is entirely in the statement language: whether Governing Council maintains its pure look-through framing on oil or begins to lean on the conditional trigger it published on 29 July. Any acknowledgement that oil has run above the July MPR assumption would be pair-bullish by widening the differential from the Canadian side — the only mechanism in this analysis by which the differential can widen. This meeting precedes the BoJ by sixteen days, so it sets the tone before Japan sets the price.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting
catalysts.rationale: The single largest scheduled event for the pair and the meeting Ueda pointed at when he said the Board would debate policy from the next meeting onward. A 25bp hike to 1.25% would compress the pair's differential from 125bp to 100bp — a 20% reduction in its entire yield support — and would confirm the 'intervals of a few months' cadence the June Summary of Opinions described, opening a path toward the board's 2% neutral. Priced at only 16-35%.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada decision and Monetary Policy Report
catalysts.rationale: The most underpriced scheduled item in the Canadian calendar and the principal risk to the bearish pair thesis. The July MPR was built on the 9 July oil futures curve, assuming Brent near $75 and WTI stabilising at $65 against an $84 market, and Governing Council has published a commitment to respond if oil-driven inflation broadens. A hawkish oil-assumption revision here would widen the pair's differential rather than narrow it — partially offset because the same MPR must cut its growth forecast for Section 338 tariffs it does not currently incorporate.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting with quarterly Outlook Report
catalysts.rationale: Falls two days after the BoC MPR, creating the tightest bilateral event cluster of the strategic window and a genuine two-day resolution of both legs. The Outlook Report will show whether FY2027 core CPI is revised above the current 2.4% as energy subsidies roll off, and cumulative BoJ hike probability by this meeting is roughly 44-60%.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada and Bank of Japan final 2026 decisions (BoC 9 Dec, BoJ 18 Dec)
catalysts.rationale: The BoC meeting is where any October MPR revision translates into action; the BoJ meeting nine days later carries an OIS-implied cumulative hike probability of roughly 81-84%. The bilateral significance is the sequence: if the BoC hikes and the BoJ hikes, the differential is unchanged at 125bp and the pair holds — but if the BoC holds and the BoJ hikes, the differential falls to 100bp and the strategic thesis is confirmed.

catalysts.event: Japan FY2027 budget and JGB issuance plan
catalysts.rationale: The FY2026 plan cut calendar-base market issuance by JPY 3.8tn and held new debt below JPY 30tn, which supported the long end. The FY2027 equivalent under a Takaichi government with a 352-seat supermajority is the key test of whether fiscal discipline survives the mandate, with the 30-year JGB already at 3.971%. A loose plan revives the fiscal-risk-premium channel that carried CAD/JPY from 105 to 117 — but now also raises the probability of further coordinated intervention.

invalidators.condition: Brent sustains above $110 for ten consecutive trading days while the BoJ holds at both the 18 September and 30 October meetings
invalidators.mechanism: The pair's two channels would align: Japan's terms of trade would approach the 69.80 record low with mineral fuel imports compounding from an already-41.9% year-on-year base, while Canada's export receipts compound and the BoC's own conditional oil trigger becomes operative — and the policy compression that carries a -0.1440 contribution would have failed to materialise
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Brent front month against $110, and BoJ post-meeting statements
invalidators.monitor_frequency: Daily for Brent, per meeting for the BoJ

invalidators.condition: CAD/JPY closes above 114.82 on a weekly basis
invalidators.mechanism: Reclaiming the converged 100-day/200-day cluster would restore the pair's long-term trend structure, flip systematic trend-following flow back to buying, and invalidate Factor 9's bearish tactical reading — while simultaneously demonstrating that the coordinated intervention has been tested and dismissed
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Weekly close versus the 114.42-114.82 moving-average cluster

invalidators.condition: The CA-JP 2-year yield spread widens beyond 155bp for five consecutive sessions
invalidators.mechanism: A 20bp widening from the current 135.3bp against a thesis built entirely on compression would signal the market has decisively rejected both the BoJ-hawkish and the BoC-anchored halves of the rate view; with only 125bp of policy carry, a 20bp widening restores 16% of the pair's yield support in a single repricing

invalidators.condition: Section 338 tariffs are deferred or withdrawn before 19 August AND Canada's July Labour Force Survey shows unemployment below 6.4%
invalidators.mechanism: The base leg's 102,495-contract leveraged short would face a squeeze with no offsetting Japanese catalyst until 20 August, and the pair's only dated bullish catalyst would fire into the thinnest positioning cushion
invalidators.monitor_indicator: USTR proclamations and Department of Finance Canada tariff pages, plus the Statistics Canada LFS release

invalidators.condition: The combined CFTC yen net short falls below 90,000 contracts while CAD/JPY remains above 112.00
invalidators.mechanism: That is the signature of a squeeze that has completed without producing a trend — the fuel is spent and the pair has not moved — which would remove Factor 4's -0.0550 tactical contribution and reduce the thesis to the rate differential alone
invalidators.monitor_indicator: CFTC Traders in Financial Futures, yen, leveraged funds plus asset managers

invalidators.condition: The 30-year JGB exceeds 4.25% while CAD/JPY simultaneously rises above 114.00
invalidators.mechanism: That combination confirms the fiscal-dominance regime — Japanese yields rising as a credit risk premium rather than a policy premium — which is the mechanism that produced 120bp of GoC-JGB spread compression alongside a 1.91% pair gain over twelve months, and would validate Factor 8's structural case over Factor 1's cyclical one
invalidators.monitor_indicator: MoF constant-maturity 30-year JGB alongside CAD/JPY spot

invalidators.condition: The Federal Reserve hikes 25bp in September or October while the BoJ holds
invalidators.mechanism: The carry regime would be re-validated at exactly the moment the yen squeeze exhausts itself; yen shorts would rebuild against a firmer dollar, and the Canadian dollar would outperform the yen on the cross because Canada's US trade linkage cushions it while Japan has no equivalent anchor
invalidators.monitor_indicator: CME FedWatch and BoJ post-meeting statements

signposts.indicator: Bank of Japan September hike probability (18 September meeting)
signposts.current_level: 16-35%, depending on source representation; cumulative OIS-implied rate of 1.21% after 18 December, i.e. 21bp
signposts.confirms_if: Rises above 50% on both representations following the 10 August Summary of Opinions or the 20 August CPI
signposts.bilateral_importance: This matters more for CAD/JPY than for any other yen cross relative to the pair's own carry, because a single 25bp hike removes 20% of a 125bp differential versus only 7% of AUD/JPY's 335bp differential
signposts.frequency: Daily, with step-changes around BoJ publications

signposts.invalidates_if: Widens beyond 155bp for five consecutive sessions
signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the pair's single most direct driver and the front-end spread matters more than the 10-year gap of 78.9bp because Japan's 2s10s of +130.4bp is nearly twice Canada's +74bp — the curve, not the level, has been doing the work

signposts.indicator: Brent crude and JKM LNG (the pair's terms-of-trade wedge)
signposts.current_level: Brent $91.82 (27 July; intramonth peak $105.32 on 23 July), JKM LNG $21.33/mmBtu, Newcastle coal $134.05/tonne
signposts.confirms_if: Brent falls below $80 for a full quarter, removing the terms-of-trade offset that contributes +0.1216 strategically
signposts.invalidates_if: Brent sustains above $110 for ten consecutive sessions
signposts.bilateral_importance: This matters more for CAD/JPY than for either currency alone because it is the only variable in the framework that acts twice in the same direction on a single pair — positively on a base currency that exports 4.3 MMb/d and negatively on a quote currency that imports roughly 99% of its oil

signposts.indicator: Combined CFTC positioning: yen net short versus Canadian dollar net short
signposts.current_level: JPY -185,047 contracts (leveraged -101,990, asset managers -83,057, 28 July report, open interest 432,366) against CAD -203,655 (leveraged -102,495, asset managers -101,160, open interest 372,447)

signposts.invalidates_if: The Canadian dollar short shrinks below -150,000 while the yen short holds beyond -170,000, or both normalise in parallel
signposts.bilateral_importance: For most pairs one leg's positioning is decisive; for CAD/JPY the two legs are at opposite percentile extremes against a common dollar, so only the differential rate of normalisation carries information
signposts.frequency: Weekly, Fridays, as at the prior Tuesday

signposts.indicator: CAD/JPY spot versus the 114.42-114.82 moving-average cluster
signposts.current_level: 111.99, which is 2.12% below the 50-day (114.42254), 2.46% below the 100-day (114.82217) and 2.45% below the 200-day (114.81054); 57th percentile of the 52-week range 104.786-117.49155
signposts.confirms_if: A daily close below 111.85 followed by weekly closes below 110.00, confirming a lower high at 117.49
signposts.invalidates_if: A weekly close above 114.82, reclaiming the converged long-average cluster
signposts.bilateral_importance: The 100-day and 200-day sit 0.012 yen apart, making this the densest systematic trigger zone on any yen cross's chart — a single level that simultaneously decides trend classification for both the medium and long term

signposts.indicator: Japan July national core CPI versus Canada CPI-trim (the inflation differential)
signposts.current_level: Japan national core 1.6% and core-core 1.7% (June), with Tokyo July core at 1.9% leading; Canada CPI-trim 1.80% and CPI-median 1.90% (June, both below target and falling)
signposts.confirms_if: Japanese national core prints at or above 1.8% on 20 August while Canadian CPI-trim stays below 1.9% on 17 August
signposts.invalidates_if: Japanese core prints at or below 1.4% while Canadian CPI-trim reverses above 2.0%
signposts.bilateral_importance: These two releases fall three days apart and jointly determine both banks' reaction functions; what matters is the crossover — the moment Japan's core exceeds Canada's, the policy differential's direction of travel becomes unambiguous
signposts.frequency: Monthly — Tokyo at month-end, Japan national around the 20th, Canada mid-month

signposts.current_level: 3.971% (30 July), within 4bp of the all-time high of 4.013% set 9 July; 10s30s +117.0bp; 20-year 3.680%
signposts.confirms_if: Holds below 4.10% while the 2-year rises above 1.60% — a bear-flattening driven by policy rather than fiscal risk
signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the mechanism that explains the pair's central anomaly — 120bp of GoC-JGB spread compression alongside a 1.91% pair gain; the Canadian 30-year at 3.99% yields essentially the same as Japan's despite four notches of rating advantage

signposts.indicator: Yen-complex implied volatility and risk reversals
signposts.current_level: Yen volatility at 13.5%, the highest among G10 peers, with implied put volatility more than four percentage points above call volatility; CAD/JPY realised approximately 13.6% (7-session) against an estimated 1M implied of 11-12%
signposts.confirms_if: The skew flattens or inverts toward yen calls while implied volatility holds above 10%, indicating the market has stopped betting on renewed yen weakness
signposts.invalidates_if: Implied volatility falls below 7% with the put skew persisting, restoring the pre-intervention carry regime
signposts.bilateral_importance: The skew is the cleanest read on whether the market believes the intervention will hold, and for CAD/JPY it is the direct measure of how expensive it is to be positioned with us versus against us given the pair's thin 125bp carry

assumptions: Spot and price-derived metrics (spot 111.99058, performance figures, 52-week range, range percentile, moving averages) come from the supplied Twelve Data daily OHLC series and are the source of truth; a discrepancy exists between the dossiers' 1 August fixing (113.08) and the price series' 31 July close (112.35), reflecting different fixing conventions.

Realised volatility is computed from supplied daily closes annualised at sqrt(252); the 20-day figure of approximately 9% is an estimate because the window straddles a regime break dominated by two observations.

Implied volatility is estimated and unverified: no CAD/JPY-specific implied volatility, risk-reversal or term-structure data was retrievable; the 1M estimate of 11-12% and 3M estimate of 9.5-10.5% are inferred from yen-complex readings adjusted for CAD/JPY's historically lower beta than USD/JPY, and Factor 9 confidence is reduced accordingly.

Forward points are derived, not quoted: no vendor CAD/JPY forward quote was retrievable; 1M/3M/6M points are computed from the +125bp policy differential under covered interest parity and will differ from true points by the unmeasured cross-currency basis.

Support and resistance levels are derived from web chart analysis per framework rules; 111.85 and 113.30 are sourced directly, 113.96 is a flipped prior support, 110.77 and the 114.42-114.82 cluster are derived from price data, and 110.00/115.00 are inferred round-number levels not directly sourced.
Cross-currency basis is a genuine data gap: no 3M JPY/USD or CAD/USD basis level was obtainable, capping Factor 10 confidence at 45 at both horizons.

Valuation methodology conflict is unresolved and both figures are reported: the CAD dossier's level-ratio REER approach implies 77.15 (flagged unusable because BIS indices are not comparable across countries in levels); the JPY dossier's deviation-from-own-mean approach implies 107.42, which we use.

Bilateral trade figures are taken directly from the supplied IMF DOTS block and not re-estimated; the mirror asymmetry between Canadian and Japanese reported figures reflects standard c.i.f./f.o.b. and timing differences rather than data error.

Weight adjustments: Factor 5 raised 0.03 at both horizons, Factor 8 raised 0.01 tactically/0.02 strategically, and Factor 10 cut 0.04 tactically/0.05 strategically; all within the +/-0.05 limit and netting to zero at both horizons.

Scoring methodology: stance scores are Bullish +1, Neutral 0, Bearish -1, multiplied by confidence/100 and by horizon weight; conviction mapping is |score| below 0.05 -> 1, 0.05-0.15 -> 2, 0.15-0.30 -> 3, 0.30-0.45 -> 4, above 0.45 -> 5.

Consensus construction: direct pair forecasts located were of mixed quality including one internally contradictory source; the cross-implied consensus of approximately 115-116 for Q4-2026 is a derived figure, not a survey median.

The coordinated Japan-US intervention is newer than both base dossiers, which were finalised 1 August and described the 30 July operation as unilateral; subsequent reporting establishes it as coordinated with the US Treasury, the first such action since 2011 — this analysis incorporates that update and it is the principal reason the pair view diverges from the CAD dossier's own long-CAD/JPY recommendation.

Scenario probabilities are subjective and follow the framework's standard 50/25/25 structure; individual invalidator probabilities are independent estimates and do not sum to 100% because conditions are not mutually exclusive.
